title: Ras to MAPK: The Kinase Cascade

generated.pipeline: extract → Gemini draft → Claude Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In PC12 cells, what different outcomes do EGF and NGF produce even though both act through Ras, Raf, MEK, and ERK?
cards.back: EGF makes PC12 cells divide, whereas NGF makes them stop dividing and grow long, nerve-like fibres.
cards.quote: epidermal growth factor (EGF) makes the cell divide, while nerve growth factor (NGF) makes it stop dividing and grow long, nerve-like fibres

cards.front: In the classical RTK–Ras–Raf–MEK–ERK cascade, what three functions can the three-kinase relay perform on a membrane signal, and what three factors shape its outcome?
cards.back: The relay can amplify, sharpen, and control a membrane signal; duration, cell context, and pathway state shape what the cascade does.
cards.quote: A three-kinase relay can amplify, sharpen, and control a membrane signal; duration, cell context, and pathway state shape what the cascade does.

cards.front: In RTK-to-Ras signalling, the adaptor Grb2 binds a phosphotyrosine on the receptor tail with its {{c1::SH2 domain}} and holds SOS with its SH3 domains.
cards.why: Grb2 bridges the activated receptor tyrosine kinase and SOS, bringing SOS to the membrane where Ras sits on its lipid anchors.
cards.quote: The adaptor Grb2 binds one with its SH2 domain and holds SOS with its SH3 domains, bringing SOS to the membrane
cards.section: Ras-GTP catches Raf at the membrane

cards.front: SOS activates Ras by acting as a {{c1::guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF)}}, making Ras release GDP so plentiful GTP can bind.
cards.quote: SOS is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF): it makes Ras release GDP so plentiful GTP takes its place.
cards.section: Ras-GTP catches Raf at the membrane

cards.front: Which two surface loops on Ras change shape when GTP occupies the nucleotide pocket instead of GDP, and how do they change?
cards.back: Switch I and switch II snap taut with GTP into a shape effectors can grip, and go slack when GDP is bound.
cards.quote: With GTP in its pocket, two surface loops on Ras—switch I and switch II—snap taut into a shape effectors can grip; with GDP they go slack.
cards.section: Ras-GTP catches Raf at the membrane

cards.front: How does SOS switch Ras on, and what turns Ras back off?
cards.back: SOS causes Ras to release GDP so more plentiful GTP takes its place; Ras stays on until it cuts that GTP back to GDP.
cards.quote: it makes Ras release GDP so plentiful GTP takes its place. Ras stays on until it cuts that GTP to GDP
cards.section: Ras-GTP catches Raf at the membrane

cards.front: Ras is not a kinase. How does Ras-GTP activate Raf?
cards.back: Ras-GTP binds Raf by contact and recruits it to the membrane, where membrane lipids and further steps help Raf open and pair side to side with another Raf.
cards.why: In a resting cell, cytosolic Raf is folded shut; normal activation requires opening and side-to-side kinase-domain pairing at the membrane.
cards.quote: Two Raf molecules then pair side to side, kinase domain beside kinase domain, which normal activation requires.
cards.section: Ras-GTP catches Raf at the membrane

cards.front: A mutant Ras lacks its lipid anchor and floats in the cytosol, yet still binds GTP and grips Raf's Ras-binding domain. What happens to Raf and MEK activation, and why?
cards.back: Raf and MEK stay inactive. Catching Raf in the cytosol fails to bring Raf to the membrane, where membrane lipids and further steps are needed for Raf to open and pair.
cards.quote: Moving Raf to the membrane is well established, but binding alone does not open Raf: membrane lipids and further steps help release the closed shape.
cards.section: Ras-GTP catches Raf at the membrane

cards.front: A mutation disables the SH3 domains of Grb2 while leaving its SH2 domain intact. After growth factor activates a receptor tyrosine kinase, what happens to Ras-GTP levels, and why?
cards.back: Ras-GTP fails to rise. Grb2 can still bind receptor phosphotyrosines via its SH2 domain, but without functional SH3 domains it cannot hold SOS and bring it to membrane-anchored Ras.
cards.quote: The adaptor Grb2 binds one with its SH2 domain and holds SOS with its SH3 domains, bringing SOS to the membrane where Ras sits on its lipid anchors
cards.section: Ras-GTP catches Raf at the membrane

cards.front: Paired Raf activates MEK by phosphorylating {{c1::two serines}} in MEK's activation loop.
cards.quote: Paired Raf phosphorylates MEK on two serines in its activation loop, the flexible stretch beside the active site
cards.section: Three kinases in series, and the two-phosphate lock

cards.front: MEK is an unusual {{c1::dual-specificity}} kinase because it phosphorylates ERK on both a threonine and a tyrosine, one residue apart, in ERK's activation loop.
cards.why: Most protein kinases target either Ser/Thr or Tyr alone, not both.
cards.quote: MEK is a dual-specificity kinase: it phosphorylates ERK (extracellular signal-regulated kinase) on both a threonine and a tyrosine, one residue apart, in ERK's activation loop.
cards.section: Three kinases in series, and the two-phosphate lock

cards.front: What is an immediate early gene (such as c-fos), and why can ERK switch it on within minutes?
cards.back: It is a gene turned on rapidly with no new protein made first, because the transcription factors and other proteins it needs are already present.
cards.why: Its product is often a transcription factor that then drives later genes.
cards.quote: a gene turned on within minutes with no new protein made first, because the proteins it needs are already present
cards.section: Three kinases in series, and the two-phosphate lock

cards.front: What three advantages does placing three kinases in series (Raf, MEK, and ERK) give the cell?
cards.back: Each tier can amplify the signal, the chain can sharpen a graded input into an all-or-none output, and separate tiers give phosphatases, feedback loops, and scaffolds multiple control points.
cards.quote: each tier can amplify, and the cascade can turn a graded input into an all-or-none output—and a third is control
cards.section: Three kinases in series, and the two-phosphate lock

cards.front: Why is the middle-to-bottom portion of the Raf–MEK–ERK pathway described as a narrow pipe ending in a wide fan?
cards.back: MEK has almost no known substrates besides ERK, whereas active ERK phosphorylates Ser/Thr-Pro sites on many cytoplasmic proteins and nuclear transcription factors such as Elk-1.
cards.quote: MEK has almost no known substrates besides ERK, making the middle of the chain a narrow pipe.
cards.section: Three kinases in series, and the two-phosphate lock

cards.front: When EGF-treated cell extracts were fractionated on chromatography columns, ERK stayed inactive with ATP alone until a separate fraction was added back. What did this rule out, and what did it show?
cards.back: It ruled out ERK activating itself by autophosphorylation and showed that a separate activator protein (later purified as MEK) is required to activate ERK.
cards.quote: An activator that parts from ERK on a column is a separate protein.
cards.section: Three kinases in series, and the two-phosphate lock

cards.front: In a dilute test tube, MEK phosphorylates ERK's threonine and tyrosine sites independently, and only doubly phosphorylated ERK is active. If raising the MEK dose increases occupancy at each site from 15% to 60%, by what factor does active ERK rise?
cards.back: 16-fold. At 15% per site, active ERK is 0.15 × 0.15 = 0.0225 (2.25%). At 60% per site, active ERK is 0.60 × 0.60 = 0.36 (36%). Ratio: 0.36 / 0.0225 = 16.
cards.why: Requiring two independent phosphorylations squares the single-site occupancy, so a 4-fold rise per site yields a 16-fold rise in active ERK.
cards.quote: Suppose MEK fills ERK's threonine and tyrosine sites independently in a test tube, and only doubly phosphorylated ERK is active.
cards.section: Three kinases in series, and the two-phosphate lock

cards.front: Assuming MEK fills ERK's threonine and tyrosine sites independently in a test tube and both phosphates are required for activity, about what percentage of each site must be phosphorylated for half (50%) of all ERK to be active?
cards.back: About 71% per site. Setting p × p = 0.50 gives p = √0.50 ≈ 0.707 (about 71%).
cards.why: Squaring keeps active ERK very low at low occupancy and requires each site to be well filled before half the ERK pool turns on.
cards.quote: it keeps doubly phosphorylated ERK very low while occupancy is low, and it means each site must be well filled before much ERK switches on.
cards.section: Three kinases in series, and the two-phosphate lock

cards.front: A phosphatase that removes only phosphotyrosine is added to active, doubly phosphorylated ERK, leaving the phosphothreonine intact. What happens to ERK activity, and why?
cards.back: ERK goes inactive. ERK's two-phosphate lock requires both the threonine and tyrosine phosphates in its activation loop; stripping either one off silences ERK.
cards.quote: ERK needs both phosphates; strip either one off with a phosphatase and ERK goes quiet.
cards.section: Three kinases in series, and the two-phosphate lock

cards.front: In the general MAP kinase plan, a MAP kinase kinase kinase activates a MAP kinase kinase, which phosphorylates a {{c1::MAP kinase}} on a threonine and a tyrosine in its activation loop.
cards.quote: a MAP kinase kinase kinase activates a MAP kinase kinase, which phosphorylates a MAP kinase on a threonine and a tyrosine in its activation loop.
cards.section: One three-tier plan, kept apart by scaffolds

cards.front: Besides the ERK cascade, what two other MAPK modules operate in animal cells, and what stimuli mainly activate them?
cards.back: The JNK and p38 modules, which respond mainly to stress such as ultraviolet light or inflammatory signals.
cards.quote: ending in JNK and p38; they use their own kinases (some shared between JNK and p38) and respond mainly to stress such as ultraviolet light or inflammatory signals.
cards.section: One three-tier plan, kept apart by scaffolds

cards.front: What two roles do scaffold proteins (such as KSR, paxillin, and MP1) play for MAPK cascades?
cards.back: They insulate modules by holding one pathway's kinases side by side (like KSR), and they localize cascades to specific sites such as focal adhesions (paxillin) or endosomes (MP1).
cards.quote: A scaffold holds one module's kinases side by side so they signal mainly to each other—as Ste5 does in yeast and KSR does for Raf, MEK and ERK
cards.section: One three-tier plan, kept apart by scaffolds

cards.front: A mutant cell expresses a form of paxillin that cannot bind Raf, MEK, or ERK, while KSR and MP1 remain normal. What happens to spatial ERK signalling, and which rule predicts this?
cards.back: ERK signalling at focal adhesions drops while KSR-scaffolded and endosomal (MP1-scaffolded) ERK signalling can still operate. This rests on the rule that scaffolds localize MAPK modules to distinct cellular sites—paxillin to focal adhesions and MP1 to endosomes.
cards.quote: Scaffolds also localize the cascade: paxillin gathers Raf, MEK and ERK at focal adhesions (where a cell grips its surroundings), and MP1 holds MEK and ERK on endosomes.
cards.section: One three-tier plan, kept apart by scaffolds

cards.front: How do ERK's fast and slow negative feedback arms differ in mechanism and speed?
cards.back: Fast feedback acts right away as ERK phosphorylates existing upstream proteins (including SOS and Raf) to weaken them; slow feedback turns on genes for dual-specificity phosphatases, requiring new protein synthesis.
cards.quote: Fast feedback: active ERK phosphorylates upstream proteins, including SOS and Raf, in ways that weaken them.
cards.section: How long the signal stays on

cards.front: In the PC12 duration model, how does ERK activity after EGF compare with ERK activity after NGF, and what limit does the evidence have?
cards.back: After EGF, ERK rises and falls within about an hour (division); after NGF, it reaches a plateau lasting hours (differentiation). However, the rule comes from one cell line, and its generality remains open.
cards.quote: In PC12 cells, ERK activity after EGF rises and falls within about an hour, whereas after NGF it climbs to a plateau lasting hours.
cards.section: How long the signal stays on

cards.front: PC12 cells are treated with a drug that blocks new protein synthesis and then stimulated with EGF. What happens to each of ERK's negative feedback arms, and why?
cards.back: Fast feedback (phosphorylation of SOS and Raf) still acts right away because those proteins are already present, while slow feedback (induction of dual-specificity phosphatases) fails because it requires new protein synthesis.
cards.quote: Slow feedback: active ERK turns on genes for dual-specificity phosphatases that strip both phosphates back off ERK, taking longer because new protein must be made.
cards.section: How long the signal stays on

cards.front: PC12 cells are engineered so EGF keeps its receptors active much longer than normal, holding ERK on for hours instead of about an hour. Under the duration hypothesis, what should the cells do, and why?
cards.back: They should stop dividing and grow nerve-like fibres, just as they do with NGF. Under the duration hypothesis, sustained ERK activity itself carries the differentiation instruction regardless of which receptor started it.
cards.quote: In 1992 Christopher Marshall and Philip Cohen's group in Dundee proposed that duration itself is the instruction—brief ERK for division, sustained ERK for differentiation
cards.section: How long the signal stays on

cards.front: Introducing the same permanently active MEK1 causes PC12 cells to grow neurites without NGF, but causes mouse NIH 3T3 fibroblasts to pile into transformed foci. What signalling principle does this contrast establish?
cards.back: Cell context shapes how a cell reads the cascade: the same unending ERK signal instructs a PC12 cell to differentiate and an NIH 3T3 fibroblast to keep dividing toward cancer.
cards.quote: Unending ERK means "differentiate" to a PC12 cell and "keep dividing" to an NIH 3T3 fibroblast.
cards.section: When the cascade is stuck on: context, cancer, and drugs

cards.front: The cancer-associated Ras {{c1::G12V}} mutation replaces glycine 12 with valine, blunting the GTP timer so Ras stays switched on.
cards.quote: found a single base change turning glycine 12 to valine—G12V, which blunts the GTP timer so Ras stays on
cards.section: When the cascade is stuck on: context, cancer, and drugs

cards.front: A tumour carries Ras G12V. What happens to ERK activity if it is treated with an EGF-receptor inhibitor versus a MEK inhibitor, and why?
cards.back: The EGF-receptor inhibitor fails because Ras G12V stays stuck on independently of the receptor and SOS above it; the MEK inhibitor shuts down ERK because it acts downstream of Ras and Raf.
cards.quote: An EGF-receptor inhibitor fails because Ras G12V stays stuck on independently of the receptor and SOS above it.
cards.section: When the cascade is stuck on: context, cancer, and drugs

cards.front: How does the B-Raf V600E mutation activate B-Raf in cutaneous melanomas, and what mechanistic question about it remains debated?
cards.back: Glutamate in the activation loop makes B-Raf active without Ras-GTP; it is often described as signalling without a partner, though mutant B-Raf can pair and whether it truly works alone is debated.
cards.quote: Glutamate in the activation loop makes B-Raf active without Ras-GTP; it is often described as signalling without a partner
cards.section: When the cascade is stuck on: context, cancer, and drugs

cards.front: Where does vemurafenib bind on B-Raf V600E, and where does trametinib bind on MEK?
cards.back: Vemurafenib fills the ATP pocket of B-Raf V600E, whereas trametinib binds an allosteric pocket beside MEK's ATP site to hold MEK inactive.
cards.quote: Vemurafenib fills the ATP pocket of B-Raf V600E, while trametinib binds MEK in an allosteric pocket beside its ATP site to hold MEK inactive.
cards.section: When the cascade is stuck on: context, cancer, and drugs

cards.front: A melanoma cell line carries B-Raf V600E and normal Ras. What happens to ERK activity after treatment with vemurafenib versus an EGF-receptor inhibitor, and why?
cards.back: Vemurafenib lowers ERK by blocking B-Raf V600E's ATP pocket, whereas an EGF-receptor inhibitor fails because glutamate in B-Raf's activation loop keeps it active without upstream Ras-GTP.
cards.quote: Vemurafenib fills the ATP pocket of B-Raf V600E, while trametinib binds MEK in an allosteric pocket beside its ATP site to hold MEK inactive.
cards.section: When the cascade is stuck on: context, cancer, and drugs

cards.front: A melanoma carries an always-active mutant Ras and normal B-Raf. What happens to ERK activity when treated with vemurafenib alone, and why?
cards.back: ERK activity rises instead of falling. Active Ras drives membrane Raf pairing, and a vemurafenib-bound Raf activates its drug-free Raf partner in the pair.
cards.why: Adding a MEK inhibitor such as trametinib cuts off signalling below Raf pairs, which is one reason Raf and MEK inhibitors are commonly combined.
cards.quote: Blocking MEK cuts off signalling below Raf pairs, one reason Raf and MEK inhibitors are commonly combined.
cards.section: When the cascade is stuck on: context, cancer, and drugs

cards.front: What are the RASopathies, and how does neurofibromatosis type 1 over-activate this pathway?
cards.back: RASopathies are developmental syndromes from mutations that mildly over-activate the Ras–MAPK pathway, causing shared facial, heart, and growth features; neurofibromatosis type 1 loses the Ras GAP neurofibromin, removing Ras's off-timer.
cards.quote: The RASopathies are developmental syndromes from mutations, inherited or new at conception, that mildly over-activate this pathway; affected children share features of the face, heart and growth.
cards.section: When the cascade is stuck on: context, cancer, and drugs

cards.front: A tumour driven by Ras G12V is treated with the MEK inhibitor trametinib. ERK activity drops sharply, but what happens to Ras-GTP recruitment of PI 3-kinase, and which pathway rule predicts this?
cards.back: Ras-GTP recruitment of PI 3-kinase would be expected to remain active. This rests on the rule that Raf is not Ras-GTP's only effector—PI 3-kinase branches directly from Ras-GTP, whereas trametinib blocks MEK downstream on the Raf–MEK–ERK branch.
cards.quote: Raf is not Ras-GTP's only target; PI 3-kinase is another, and it is the next lesson.
cards.section: When the cascade is stuck on: context, cancer, and drugs

cards.front: How does the immediate early protein c-Fos function as a delayed persistence reader for ERK duration in fibroblasts?
cards.back: Newly made c-Fos is short-lived unless ERK and the ERK-activated kinase RSK are still active to phosphorylate and stabilize it, so only sustained ERK lets c-Fos drive later genes.
cards.quote: the immediate early protein c-Fos is short-lived unless ERK and RSK (a kinase ERK activates) phosphorylate it
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In PC12 cells, always-on MEK1 drives neurite growth without NGF, whereas an interfering MEK1 that cannot be activated blocks growth-factor-driven differentiation. What distinct logical conclusion does each mutant establish?
cards.back: Always-on MEK1 shows MEK is sufficient to trigger differentiation without NGF or its other pathways; interfering MEK1 shows MEK is necessary because no other pathway can stand in for it.
cards.quote: Always-on MEK1 mimics a sustained NGF signal without NGF or its other pathways, and drove neurite growth alone (showing MEK is sufficient).
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In mouse fibroblasts, always-active Ras alone gives many foci, always-active Ras together with a MEK that cannot be activated gives none, and always-active MEK together with a Ras that cannot load GTP gives many. What order of Ras and MEK do these results fit, and by what logic?
cards.back: Ras acts above MEK, and Ras needs MEK in order to transform. Blocking MEK cancels always-active Ras (so MEK is required downstream of Ras), whereas blocking Ras does not cancel always-active MEK (so MEK acts below Ras).
cards.quote: Always-on MEK1 mimics a sustained NGF signal without NGF or its other pathways, and drove neurite growth alone (showing MEK is sufficient).
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Suppose fibroblasts express a mutant c-Fos that stays stable without needing phosphorylation by ERK or RSK. How would a brief, 1-hour EGF pulse of ERK activity now affect later-gene activation, and which circuit rule explains this?
cards.back: Even the brief ERK pulse would be expected to switch on later genes normally restricted to sustained ERK. This rests on the delayed persistence-reader rule: c-Fos instability normally filters out brief signals because ERK must remain active after c-Fos synthesis to stabilize it.
cards.quote: Use a gene product made after a delay that survives only if ERK is still active.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: What assumption behind the dilute test-tube p² switch for ERK may break down inside living cells, and what is the effect?
cards.back: The calculation assumes MEK phosphorylates ERK in two separate encounters with release in between; inside living cells (such as HeLa cells), crowding and scaffolds can make phosphorylation nearly one step, lowering steepness.
cards.quote: The worked calculation assumes MEK phosphorylates ERK in two separate encounters, releasing singly phosphorylated ERK in between, as in dilute test tubes.
cards.section: Does the two-phosphate lock stay steep in living cells?

cards.front: If crowding inside a cell makes MEK phosphorylate both sites on ERK in nearly one binding encounter rather than two independent encounters, how does the rise in active ERK change when encounter probability triples, and which rule explains this?
cards.back: Active ERK would rise closer to 3-fold than 9-fold, losing the steep switch-like jump. This rests on the two-phosphate lock rule: squared steepness requires two independent encounters, so collapsing them into nearly one step makes output track input linearly.
cards.quote: Inside cells, scaffolds and crowding can change that: in HeLa cells, crowding appears to make phosphorylation nearly one step, lowering steepness, and how widely that holds is open.
cards.section: Does the two-phosphate lock stay steep in living cells?

cards.front: Among the RASopathies, mutations in {{c1::PTPN11 (the phosphatase SHP2)}} account for about half of Noonan syndrome cases, whereas HRAS mutations cause Costello syndrome.
cards.why: Other RASopathy genes in the same pathway include SOS1 and RAF1 (Noonan), BRAF and MEK genes (cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome), and neurofibromin loss (NF1).
cards.quote: PTPN11 (the phosphatase SHP2) in about half of Noonan syndrome cases and SOS1 and RAF1 in some others, HRAS in Costello syndrome
cards.section: Genes behind the RASopathies

cards.front: Why do mutations in different genes—such as losing the Ras GAP neurofibromin in NF1 or mildly activating SOS1, HRAS, RAF1, BRAF, or MEK—cause overlapping developmental features in the RASopathies?
cards.back: Each gene sits on the same Ras–Raf–MEK–ERK relay, so disabling Ras's off-timer or activating any upstream GEF, Ras, Raf, or MEK tier converges on mild over-activation of ERK output. This rests on the serial-cascade rule that signals flow through one shared chain.
cards.quote: and loss of the Ras GAP neurofibromin in neurofibromatosis type 1.
cards.section: Genes behind the RASopathies
